definition.text: A way of installing changes by keeping a live production environment and an idle staging copy, then swapping the two so the staged version goes live.

facts.text: Two servers or environments are kept, one blue and one green; only one handles requests at a time, for example the one DNS points to, while the other is a staging server on a private network.
Changes are installed on the non-live environment and tested through the private network; once verified, it is swapped with the live one and the changes go live.
Rollback is quick: traffic is simply routed back to the previous live environment, which never received the deployed changes.
Because requests move instantly from one environment to the other, ideally no request goes unfulfilled, so downtime is reduced.
The cost is running two environments at once; duplicate infrastructure, even temporarily, can be prohibitive for smaller organizations.
Complex database migrations are harder, since blue and green must hold consistent data; migration tools that keep both environments backward compatible are a common solution.
Kubernetes supports blue-green deployment through multiple deployments and services that route traffic between the blue and green environments.
Blue-green is often contrasted with the canary release and resembles A/B testing; it suits high-stake updates.

definition.text: Deployment strategies are different ways of replacing a running application version with a new one, each managing the update differently.

facts.text: Recreate terminates all existing instances at once and then creates new instances with the updated version; it suits non-critical applications or early development.
A rolling update replaces instances one by one, keeping availability high during the process; it suits periodic releases.
A canary release sends the new version to a subset of users or servers for testing before broader deployment, to validate its impact on a subset of users.
Shadow deployment redirects a copy of live traffic to the new version so it can be tested without affecting production users.
Shadow is the most complex strategy, because it needs mock services that interact with the new version.
Blue-green keeps two identical environments, one with the current version and one with the updated version, and switches traffic from blue to the prepared green environment.
A/B testing runs several versions at once on different users to compare performance or user experience, so it aims at optimizing user experience.
Another list of the most-used deployment strategies names big bang, rolling, blue-green, canary and feature toggle deployment.

definition.text: The twelve-factor app is a set of twelve best-practice principles for building modern applications that are reliable, scalable and manageable.

facts.text: Keep all code in one place under version control such as Git, and list every dependency the app needs so it is easy to install.
Keep settings such as database credentials separate from code, so they can change without rewriting code.
Treat other services, such as databases or payment processors, as separate components the app connects to.
Separate the stages of preparing the app, releasing it and running it in production.
Design processes so that no part relies on a specific computer or its memory, and expose the app through a network port without storing critical information on a single machine.
Handle more work by adding more copies of the same process, and make each process start quickly and shut down gracefully.
Keep development very similar to production to avoid surprises, and record what the app does in logs so issues can be understood and fixed.
Run special administrative tasks separately from the app itself.

definition.text: Running a container with Docker means the client asks the daemon to pull an image from a registry, create a container from it and start it.

facts.text: Docker has three components: a client that talks to the daemon, a host whose daemon listens for API requests, and a registry that stores images.
The Docker daemon manages Docker objects such as images, containers, networks and volumes; Docker Hub is a public registry anyone can use.
When docker run executes, Docker pulls the image from the registry, creates a new container and allocates a read-write filesystem to it.
Docker then creates a network interface that connects the container to the default network, and starts the container.

definition.text: Virtual machines virtualize hardware and each carry a guest operating system, while containers virtualize the operating system and carry only the application and its dependencies.

facts.text: In traditional virtualization a hypervisor virtualizes physical hardware, so each virtual machine holds a guest OS, a virtual copy of the hardware the OS needs, and the application with its libraries and dependencies.
Containers virtualize the operating system instead of the hardware, so each contains only the application and its dependencies, which makes it much more lightweight than a VM.
Containers share the OS kernel and use a fraction of the memory VMs require.
Containers are lightweight and use just the computing resources needed, whereas VMs raise hardware utilization by placing many virtual servers on one physical server.

definition.text: A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, is software, firmware or hardware that creates and runs virtual machines.

facts.text: The machine a hypervisor runs on is the host and each virtual machine is a guest; the hypervisor presents guest operating systems with a virtual platform and manages their execution.
It treats CPU, memory and storage as a pool of resources that can be reallocated between existing guests or new virtual machines.
Unlike an emulator, the guest executes most instructions on native hardware; this contrasts with OS-level virtualization, where containers must share a single kernel.
Type-1, native or bare-metal hypervisors run directly on the host's hardware to control it and manage guest operating systems; examples are Hyper-V, Xen and VMware ESXi.
Type-2 hypervisors run on a conventional operating system like any other program, with the virtual machine monitor as a host process; examples are VirtualBox and VMware Workstation.

Running several operating systems concurrently improves robustness: if one crashes the others keep working, and experimental versions can be debugged without jeopardizing the stable production system.
Modern hypervisors use hardware-assisted virtualization; Intel and AMD released their first x86 processors with hardware virtualisation in 2005 (Intel VT-x and AMD-V).
Paravirtualization instead modifies the guest operating system to make a call to the hypervisor, a hypercall, rather than executing machine I/O instructions that the hypervisor simulates.

definition.text: Docker is a platform that packages software into containers using operating system-level virtualization.

facts.text: Docker automates deploying applications inside lightweight containers so they run consistently across computing environments; its core software for running and managing containers is Docker Engine.
Containers are isolated from one another, bundle their own software, libraries and configuration files, and can communicate through well-defined channels.
All containers share one operating system kernel, so they use fewer resources than virtual machines, and a single server or virtual machine can run several containers at once.
On Linux, Docker uses kernel isolation features such as cgroups and namespaces plus a union-capable file system such as OverlayFS, avoiding the overhead of starting and maintaining virtual machines.
Namespaces mostly isolate an application's view of its environment, including process trees, network, user IDs and mounted file systems, while cgroups limit memory and CPU.
Docker on macOS runs its containers inside a Linux virtual machine.
The Docker daemon, dockerd, is a persistent process that manages containers and listens for Docker Engine API requests; the docker command-line client lets users interact with daemons.
The main classes of Docker objects are images, containers and services; a container is a standardized, encapsulated environment that runs applications.

definition.text: A container image is a read-only template used to build containers, and a registry is a repository that stores and serves images.

facts.text: A Docker image is a read-only template used to build containers, and images are used to store and ship applications.
A Dockerfile is a text file that commonly specifies the Linux distribution of an image, the installation commands for the language runtime and the application source code.
A registry is a repository for images; clients connect to it to download ('pull') images for use or upload ('push') images they have built.
Docker Hub is the default registry where Docker looks for images, and it is a public registry that anyone can use.
Registries can also create notifications based on events.

definition.text: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications.

facts.text: It uses YAML files to configure the application's services and creates and starts all the containers with a single command.
The docker-compose.yml file defines an application's services and their configuration options, such as the path of the Dockerfile used to build one.
The docker compose command-line utility runs commands on several containers at once, for example building images, scaling containers or restarting stopped ones.

definition.text: Docker Swarm provides native clustering for Docker containers, turning a group of Docker engines into a single virtual Docker engine.

facts.text: A Docker service lets containers be scaled across multiple Docker daemons; the resulting set of cooperating daemons that communicate through the Docker API is a swarm, integrated into Docker Engine since Docker 1.12.
Docker manages swarms with the Raft consensus algorithm, so a majority of Swarm nodes must agree before an update is performed.
The docker stack tool manages Swarm services with a configuration file very like docker-compose.yml, and can manage a Swarm cluster across multiple machines.

definition.text: A container runtime is the software responsible for the lifecycle of containers, including launching, reconciling and killing them.

facts.text: Every Kubernetes node must run a container runtime; the kubelet talks to it through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), which decouples maintaining core Kubernetes from any one runtime.
containerd and CRI-O are widely used CRI-compliant runtimes; Kubernetes was originally tightly coupled to Docker and dropped official Docker support as a runtime with v1.24 in May 2022.

Since version 1.11 Docker Engine has been built on containerd and runc, the reference implementation of the Open Container Initiative runtime specification; containerd uses runc by default but can use other runtimes.

definition.text: Kubernetes, also known as K8s, is an open-source container orchestration system for automating software deployment, scaling and management.

facts.text: Kubernetes assembles one or more computers, virtual machines or bare metal, into a cluster that can run workloads in containers; the software consists of a control plane and the nodes on which applications run.
It defines building blocks called primitives that deploy, maintain and scale applications based on CPU, memory or custom metrics.
Kubernetes is loosely coupled and extensible; its internal components and the extensions and containers running on it all rely on the Kubernetes API.
The platform controls compute and storage resources by defining them as objects that can be managed as such.
In production the control plane usually runs across multiple computers and a cluster runs multiple nodes, providing fault tolerance and high availability.
Kubernetes is commonly used to host microservice-based systems, because it and its ecosystem of tools provide the capabilities microservice architectures need.
Its design is greatly influenced by Google's internal system Borg.

Kubernetes is not mere orchestration, which executes a defined workflow of first A, then B, then C; it is a set of independent, composable control processes that continuously drive the current state toward the desired state.

definition.text: The Kubernetes control plane manages the cluster's workload and its worker nodes and directs communication across the system.

facts.text: The control plane manages the worker nodes and the pods in the cluster; in production it usually runs across multiple computers for fault tolerance and high availability.
The API server serves the Kubernetes API using JSON over HTTPS as both the internal and external interface, and every operation on pods is executed by talking to it.
The API server processes and validates REST requests and updates the state of API objects in etcd, which lets clients configure workloads and containers across worker nodes.
etcd is the key-value store that serves as the backing store for all cluster data.

The scheduler selects the node an unscheduled pod runs on, based on resource availability and other constraints, and tracks allocation so workload is not scheduled beyond a node's available resources.
The controller manager runs the controllers, including the node, job, EndpointSlice and ServiceAccount controllers, as a single process.
Kubernetes follows a primary/replica architecture, with components divided between those that manage an individual node and those that form the control plane.

definition.text: etcd is a persistent, lightweight, distributed key-value data store, originally developed as part of CoreOS.

facts.text: In Kubernetes it is the backing store for all cluster data, reliably holding the cluster's configuration and so representing the overall state of the cluster at any given point in time.
During a network partition etcd favors consistency over availability, because consistency is crucial for correctly scheduling and operating services.
The API server uses etcd's watch API to monitor the cluster, roll out critical configuration changes and restore any divergence of the cluster back to the desired state declared in etcd.

definition.text: A Kubernetes controller is a reconciliation loop that drives the actual cluster state toward the desired state by creating, updating and deleting the resources it manages.

facts.text: Objects record the desired state in a spec field, while the controller of the resource keeps a status field describing the current state up to date.
For example, if an operator declares three instances of a pod and the Deployment controller finds only two running, it schedules the creation of another instance.
The ReplicaSet controller runs a specified number of copies of a pod across the cluster and creates replacement pods if the underlying node fails.

The DaemonSet controller ensures a pod runs on every node, which suits workloads tied to the host such as log collection, ingress controllers and storage services; the Job controller runs pods to completion, as in a batch job.
Label selectors often form part of a controller's definition, specifying the set of pods it manages.
The controller manager is one process managing several core controllers, and custom controllers can be installed to extend Kubernetes together with custom resources.

definition.text: A Kubernetes node, also called a worker or minion, is a machine where containers are deployed.

facts.text: Every cluster has at least one worker node, which hosts the pods that are the components of the application workload.
Every node must run a container runtime plus components that connect its containers to the network.
The kubelet is an agent on each node that ensures the containers of its pods are running and healthy, starting, stopping and maintaining them as the control plane directs.

The kubelet reports node status to the API server in heartbeat messages every few seconds; when the control plane detects a node failure, a higher-level controller is expected to launch the pods on another healthy node.
kube-proxy runs on each node as a network proxy and load balancer supporting the service abstraction, routing traffic to the appropriate container by the IP and port of the incoming request.

definition.text: A pod is the basic deployable unit in Kubernetes, made of one or more containers co-located on the same node.

facts.text: The pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes administers, and in the most common use case each pod has a single container.
Each pod has a unique IP address within the cluster, shared by every container inside it, so applications can use ports without the risk of conflict.
Containers within a pod have a shared context and can reference each other.
Higher-level workload abstractions let users declaratively manage groups of pods instead of managing individual pods themselves.
Containers in a Pod share one network namespace, IP address and port space and reach each other on localhost; containers in different Pods have distinct IP addresses and talk over IP networking.
A Pod can declare shared storage volumes that all its containers can use, and volumes let a Pod's data survive a container restart.

Pods are relatively ephemeral and disposable, so they are rarely created directly: a workload resource such as a Deployment creates them, replicates them for scale, and replaces them when a node fails.
Static Pods are supervised directly by the kubelet on one node, without the API server observing them; their main use is running a self-hosted control plane.

definition.text: A ReplicaSet keeps a stable set of replica pods running at any given time, and a Deployment is the higher-level mechanism that manages ReplicaSets.

facts.text: A ReplicaSet is often used to guarantee the availability of a specified number of identical pods, and uses a selector to identify the pods associated with it.
The ReplicationController was the predecessor of the ReplicaSet and was deprecated in favor of it to make use of set-based label selectors.
The ReplicaSet controller manages the scale of the ReplicaSet, while the Deployment controller manages what happens to the ReplicaSet, such as whether an update is rolled out or rolled back.
Scaling a Deployment up or down changes the declared state of the ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet controller carries out that change.
A Deployment manages a set of Pods, usually for a workload that keeps no state; you declare the desired state and the Deployment controller changes the actual state to match it at a controlled rate.

Updating the Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet that is scaled up as the old one is scaled down; an update during a rollout stops the earlier rollout and rolls over to the newest ReplicaSet without waiting.
A Deployment's revision history is kept in its old ReplicaSets, 10 by default, so a bad rollout can be undone; once an old ReplicaSet is deleted, that revision can no longer be rolled back to.

A Deployment is progressing, complete or failed to progress; progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) sets how long to wait before reporting failure, and a failed Deployment can still be scaled, rolled back or paused.

definition.text: A StatefulSet is a Kubernetes controller that enforces uniqueness and ordering among the instances of a pod so that stateful applications can run.

facts.text: Scaling stateless applications only means adding more pods, but stateful workloads are harder because state must be preserved when a pod restarts and may need to be redistributed when scaling.
Databases are stateful; in high-availability mode many have a primary and secondary instances, so the ordering of instances matters.
Applications such as Apache Kafka distribute data among their brokers, so one broker is not the same as another and instance uniqueness matters.

definition.text: A Kubernetes service is a set of pods that work together, such as one tier of a multi-tier application, giving them a stable address.

facts.text: The pods that make up a service are defined by a label selector.
Service discovery gives the service a stable IP address and DNS name and load balances traffic round-robin across the matching pods, even as failures move pods from machine to machine.
Kubernetes offers two modes of service discovery: environment variables or Kubernetes DNS.
By default a service is exposed inside the cluster, for example back-end pods balancing requests from front-end pods, but it can also be exposed outside the cluster.
On each node, kube-proxy routes traffic coming in from the service and forwards requests to the correct containers.
Pods are ephemeral and the set of healthy Pods changes from moment to moment, so frontends cannot track backend IPs; a Service decouples them by giving the group one stable endpoint.
EndpointSlices hold slices of a Service's backing endpoints; a new slice starts once all existing ones have at least 100 endpoints, whereas the older Endpoints API truncates beyond 1000 endpoints.
Without a selector, a Service plus hand-made EndpointSlices can abstract backends outside the cluster, such as an external database or a Service in another namespace or cluster.

definition.text: ConfigMaps and Secrets are two closely related Kubernetes mechanisms for storing configuration, so that changes can be made without rebuilding the application.

facts.text: Secrets are designed for confidential data such as certificates, registry credentials, passwords and ssh keys, but they are not encrypted at rest by default and need extra setup to be fully secured.
A pod receives the data as environment variables or as files in a mounted volume, and volume mounts support automatic reloading without restarting the container.
A ConfigMap or Secret is sent to a node only if a pod on that node requires it, is held only in memory, and is deleted when that pod is deleted.

definition.text: Labels are keys that Kubernetes clients attach to any API object, such as pods and nodes, and label selectors are queries that resolve to the matching objects.

facts.text: A service's label selector chooses the pod instances that its router or load balancer sends traffic to.
Changing pod labels or a service's selector controls which pods receive traffic, which can support deployment patterns such as blue-green deployments or A/B testing.
This dynamic control over which resources implement a service gives the infrastructure loose coupling.

definition.text: Container filesystems are ephemeral by default, so data that must outlive a container needs a volume that provides persistent storage.

facts.text: In Kubernetes a container's filesystem is wiped when the container restarts, which is limiting for anything but trivial applications.
A Kubernetes volume provides persistent storage and shared disk space for the containers in a pod, and the same volume can be mounted at different points by different containers.
A Docker volume likewise lets data persist independently, remaining after a container is deleted or re-created.

Kubernetes was historically suited only to stateless services; databases need persistence, and the Container Storage Interface separated the code for external storage systems from the core Kubernetes code base.

definition.text: A Kubernetes Operator is the combination of custom resources and custom controllers that automates how a particular application is run.

facts.text: The Kubernetes API can be extended with Custom Resources, declared through Custom Resource Definitions that can be registered and unregistered without restarting a running cluster.
Custom controllers observe custom resources and reconcile the cluster toward the declared desired state, giving users a declarative API.
Operators capture the knowledge of a human operator and automate it, for example taking and restoring backups or handling upgrades together with schema or configuration changes.

definition.text: A container is an isolated user-space instance that the operating system kernel allows alongside others, packaging an application with its dependencies so it runs the same in any environment.

facts.text: In OS-level virtualization the kernel allows several isolated user-space instances; programs inside a container can only see the container's contents and the devices assigned to it, and each container gets a subset of the computer's resources.
A container packages code and all its dependencies, such as specific runtime and library versions, so the application runs quickly and reliably from one computing environment to another.

This decoupling from the environment lets container-based applications be deployed easily and consistently, and gives developers and operations teams a clear separation of responsibility between application logic and deployment.
Besides isolation, the kernel often provides resource-management features that limit the impact of one container's activity on others; Linux containers rely on Linux namespaces and cgroups.

Containers cost less than full virtualization because programs use the operating system's normal system call interface and need no emulation or intermediate virtual machine; they are lightweight and use just the resources needed.

The trade-off is flexibility: a container cannot host a guest operating system different from the host's, or a different guest kernel, so on Linux other distributions are fine but Windows cannot be hosted.

Typical uses are securely allocating finite hardware resources among many mutually distrusting users, and consolidating server hardware by moving services from separate hosts into containers on one server.

definition.text: Namespaces and cgroups are the Linux kernel features that isolate containers: namespaces control what a process can see, cgroups how much of the system's resources it can use.

facts.text: Namespaces partition kernel resources so that one set of processes sees one set of resources and another set sees a different set, giving each the illusion of being the sole user of the system.
Cgroups dictate how much of the system a process can use, such as CPU, memory and disk I/O limits, while namespaces dictate what it may see; together they underpin Docker, Kubernetes, LXC and Podman.

A system begins with one initial namespace of each type shared by all processes; processes can create new namespaces or join existing ones, nesting isolation boundaries, over resources such as process IDs, hostnames, user IDs and network interfaces.
As of Linux 5.6 there are eight kinds: mount, process ID (pid), network, inter-process communication (ipc), UTS (hostname and NIS domain name), user, cgroup and time.

A PID namespace gives processes an independent set of IDs; the host sees every container process under a different PID, and the first process inside is PID 1, whose exit makes the kernel kill all others in that namespace.

A network namespace virtualizes the network stack with its own IP addresses, routing table and firewall rules; connectivity is usually given by a veth pair with one end in the container and the other bridged on the host.

User namespaces map user and group IDs between container and host, so a process can be root (UID 0) inside the container yet an unprivileged ID on the host; they are the backbone of unprivileged containers.

Namespaces are created with the clone system call using flags such as CLONE_NEWPID or CLONE_NEWNET, or with unshare; setns lets a running process enter an existing namespace, and the kernel destroys a namespace nothing references.

definition.text: A virtual machine is the virtualization or emulation of a computer system that provides the functionality of a physical computer.

facts.text: A virtual machine runs as a virtual computer system with its own CPU, memory, network interface and storage, created on a physical hardware system; implementations may use specialized hardware, software or both.
The physical hardware running the VM is the host and the emulated machine is the guest; one host can emulate several guests, each running a different operating system.
VMs are isolated from the rest of the system, several can share one piece of hardware, and they can be moved between host servers to match demand or use resources more efficiently.
System virtual machines substitute for a real machine and can execute entire operating systems, whereas process virtual machines run a single program in a platform-independent environment.

A process VM runs as a normal application inside a host OS, exists only while its process runs, and lets a program execute the same way on any platform; the Java virtual machine is a well-known example.

Server consolidation is a top reason for VMs: most deployments use only a small part of a server's physical resources, so many virtual servers can be placed on each physical server to improve utilization.
Because a VM is isolated, what runs inside cannot interfere with the host, which suits testing new applications, setting up production environments and isolating applications for security.

definition.text: A snapshot is the state of a virtual machine, and generally its storage devices, at an exact point in time, which can be restored later.

facts.text: Restoring a snapshot effectively undoes any later changes, which makes snapshots a useful backup technique before a risky operation.
Each snapshot creates a new file used as an overlay for its predecessors: new data is written to the topmost overlay, and reads scan the overlay hierarchy to find the most recent version.
Snapshots can be moved to another host machine with its own hypervisor; stopping the VM temporarily, snapshotting, moving and resuming it on the new host is known as migration.
Failover, similar to migration, allows the VM to continue operating if its host fails.

definition.text: A feature toggle is a condition in the code that enables or disables a feature at runtime, as an alternative to maintaining multiple feature branches.

facts.text: Toggles are essentially variables used inside conditional statements, so the code block behind them can be switched on or off; they are also called feature flags, switches or gates.
An unfinished feature can be merged into the main branch and hidden behind a toggle, then switched on in a test environment, or in production on demand for some or all users.
Toggles shorten integration cycles, reduce the effort of merging features into and out of the productive branch, and allow many small incremental versions, so releasing often becomes easier.
Toggles make advanced rollout strategies such as canary rollout and A/B testing easier to handle, and they support continuous delivery even when releases are not deployed to production continuously.

Toggles are classified as release, experiment, ops and permissioning toggles, which differ by how long they should live; an ops toggle can act as a kill switch that disables a feature at runtime during an incident.
Toggle debt arises when a feature is toggled on permanently and dead code remains; it adds overhead, and the code must be removed carefully so other parts are not disturbed.

Toggles need lifecycle management beyond the conditionals: commonly reported practices are recording metadata for each toggle, defining a default value, logging changes and using dedicated tools to manage them.
Martin Fowler says a release toggle should be your last choice for putting features into production; it is better to break the feature into smaller parts that can each be released safely.

definition.text: A canary release exposes a new version or feature to a small set of users first, so it can be tested incrementally before a wider rollout.

facts.text: A canary sends the new version to a subset of users or servers for testing before broader deployment, to validate its impact; blue-green deployment is often contrasted with it.
A canary release turns the feature on for a sampled cohort, such as 1% of users, while everyone else stays off.
Feature flags are an alternative way to run canary launches and allow targeting by geographic location or by user attributes.
If the feature's performance is not satisfactory, it can be rolled back without adverse effects.
The SRE book calls it a best practice to test a new release on a small subset of a typical workload; the open questions are how long to wait and how big the canary should be.
In Google's release process, a typical canary deployment starts a few jobs in the production environment after system tests complete.
In Kubernetes a canary is done with multiple Deployments, one per release; Services are a common fit, and a release_track label with values such as canary and production tells pods apart.

definition.text: Continuous delivery is a software engineering approach in which teams produce software in short cycles, ensuring that it can be reliably released at any time.

facts.text: It aims to build, test and release software with greater speed and frequency, cutting the cost, time and risk of delivering changes by allowing more incremental updates to production.
Every commit is built and packaged by a build server and tested by several techniques before it can be marked releasable, so any commit may be released to customers at any point.

The deployment pipeline is a set of validations a change must pass on its way to release; its purpose is visibility, feedback and continually deploying any version to any environment through full automation.
Continuous delivery brings the pain forward, tackling tough tasks early to foster automation and swift issue detection, and it needs a straightforward, repeatable deployment process.
Feature toggles let code that is not yet ready for users be committed early; long-lived branches become impractical because a releasable artifact must be built early from a single branch.

Applications must meet architecturally significant requirements such as deployability, modifiability and testability; microservices are often used, improving deployment independence, deployment time and zero-downtime deployment.
Deployment scripts are tested repeatedly before production, and frequent releases carry fewer changes each, so problems are easier to find and fix and their impact lasts a shorter time.

Obstacles include a lack of test automation, differences between development, test and production environments, tests that need a human oracle, and regulated domains that require customer-side or on-site testing.

definition.text: CI/CD combines the practices of continuous integration and continuous delivery or, less often, continuous deployment.

facts.text: A CI/CD pipeline is three processes in order: frequent merging of small changes into a main branch, producing software in short cycles so it can be released at any time, and automatic rollout of new functionality.
CI/CD services compile the incremental code changes, link and package them into deliverables; automated tests verify the functionality and automated deployment services deliver it to end users.
The aim is early defect discovery, higher productivity and faster release cycles, in contrast with traditional methods that integrated a collection of updates into one large batch before deploying.
CI/CD bridges the gaps between teams, development and operations by enforcing automation in building, testing and deployment, and forms the backbone of modern DevOps operations.
Small teams can be more productive with one repository and one pipeline, whereas larger organizations may have separate repositories and pipelines for each team or even each service.

Least privilege is hard to apply to pipeline permissions because the architecture is dynamic; administrators may allow more permissive permissions while adding compensating security controls to limit the blast radius.

definition.text: Cgroups, short for control groups, is a Linux kernel feature that limits, accounts for and isolates the resource usage (CPU, memory, disk I/O and so on) of a collection of processes.

facts.text: A control group is a collection of processes bound by the same criteria and associated with a set of parameters or limits; groups are hierarchical, each inheriting limits from its parent.
The kernel exposes controllers, also called subsystems, through the cgroup interface; for example the memory controller limits memory use and cpuacct accounts CPU usage.
Groups can be capped at a memory limit (including file system cache), I/O bandwidth, CPU quota, CPU set or open files, and some groups can get a larger share of CPU or disk I/O.
Cgroups also measure a group's resource usage, for example for billing, and can freeze groups of processes and checkpoint and restart them.
Both versions act through a pseudo-filesystem, with v2 mounted by convention on /sys/fs/cgroup; creating a subgroup is just creating a new directory, and its control files appear automatically.
Cgroup v2 has a single process hierarchy and works on processes rather than threads, whereas v1 allowed multiple hierarchies; the first kernel supporting v2 was Linux 4.5.
Docker, LXC, systemd and Kubernetes use cgroups indirectly or directly, and since Linux 4.19 the out-of-memory killer can kill a whole cgroup as a single unit to keep the workload intact.

definition.text: chroot is a Unix command and system call that changes the apparent root directory for the current process and its children.

facts.text: A program run in the modified environment, called a chroot jail, cannot name and therefore normally cannot access files outside the designated directory tree.
It is used to build and test software in a chroot holding only its expected dependencies, which prevents linkage skew, and to run legacy software whose libraries would clash with the host's.
Chroot is not designed to stop privileged users: on most systems a chrooted program with enough privilege can chroot again to break out, and it does not limit I/O, bandwidth, disk space or CPU time.
Container isolation can be seen as an advanced implementation of chroot; FreeBSD expanded the concept into jails to make it useful for virtualization.

definition.text: Infrastructure as code is managing and provisioning data center resources through machine-readable definition files rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools.

facts.text: The infrastructure covers bare-metal servers, virtual machines and their configuration; instead of building a configuration by hand, a pre-set one is applied to a machine.
Definitions live in version control; treating infrastructure like software, reviewed and deployed automatically, reduces manual errors and lets teams reproduce environments reliably.
Its value falls into cost, speed and risk: automation removes human error such as manual misconfiguration, which can decrease downtime and increase reliability.
The declarative approach defines the desired state and the system works out what to do; the imperative approach lists the commands to run in order. IaC more often uses declarative definitions.
In the push method the controlling system sends instructions directly to the server; in the pull method the server retrieves its own instructions from the controlling system.
Tools include CFEngine, Puppet, Chef, SaltStack, Ansible and Terraform: CFEngine and Chef pull their configuration, Puppet and Ansible can push or pull, and Terraform pushes.
Automation and collaboration are central to DevOps, and infrastructure automation tools are often components of a DevOps toolchain; IaC gets developers more involved in defining configuration.
IaC templates themselves need security review: a 2020 cloud threat report identified around 200,000 potential vulnerabilities in infrastructure-as-code templates.

title: Container orchestration
article: doc>kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview#Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do

definition.text: Container orchestration automates deploying, scaling and managing containers so that, for example, a container that goes down is replaced by another without downtime.

facts.text: In production the containers running applications must be managed to avoid downtime; Kubernetes provides a framework to run distributed systems resiliently, taking care of scaling, failover and deployment patterns.
Kubernetes can expose a container by DNS name or its own IP address, and load balances and distributes network traffic when traffic to a container is high so the deployment stays stable.
Automated rollouts and rollbacks: you describe the desired state of deployed containers and Kubernetes changes the actual state to match it at a controlled rate.
Automatic bin packing: you give Kubernetes a cluster of nodes and tell it how much CPU and memory each container needs, and it fits containers onto the nodes to make the best use of resources.
Self-healing: Kubernetes restarts failed containers, replaces them, kills containers that fail a user-defined health check, and does not advertise them to clients until they are ready to serve.
It scales applications up and down with a command, a UI or automatically based on CPU usage, and can automatically mount a storage system of your choice such as local storage or a public cloud.
Secrets and configuration can be deployed and updated without rebuilding container images and without exposing secrets in the stack configuration.

Kubernetes is not an all-inclusive PaaS: it works at the container level, its default solutions are optional and pluggable, it does not build applications, and it has no built-in databases or message buses.

definition.text: Applications moved from physical servers to virtual machines to containers as each step gave better resource boundaries and utilization.

facts.text: On physical servers an application's resources could not be bounded, so one application could take most of them and others underperform; one application per server did not scale because resources were underused and servers were costly.
Virtualization runs several virtual machines on one server's CPU, isolating applications and improving utilization and scalability, but each VM is a full machine with its own operating system.

Containers relax isolation to share the operating system, so they are lightweight; each has its own filesystem, share of CPU, memory and process space, and is portable across clouds and OS distributions.
Containers add faster image creation than VM images, frequent builds with quick rollbacks thanks to image immutability, consistency from laptop to cloud, and resource isolation with high density.

title: Rolling update
article: doc>kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment#Writing a Deployment Spec > Strategy > Rolling Update Deployment

definition.text: A rolling update replaces instances of the old version one by one with the new version, keeping the application available throughout.

facts.text: A Deployment's strategy type is RollingUpdate, the default, or Recreate; a rolling update gradually scales down the old ReplicaSets and scales up the new one. It suits periodic releases.
Recreate kills all existing Pods before creating new ones; it suits non-critical applications or early development.
maxUnavailable caps the Pods that may be unavailable during the update, as a number or a percentage of desired Pods; the default is 25% and a percentage is rounded down.
maxSurge caps the Pods that may be created above the desired number, as a number or a percentage; the default is 25% and a percentage is rounded up.
With maxUnavailable at 30%, at least 70% of desired Pods stay available throughout; with maxSurge at 30%, the total of old and new Pods never exceeds 130% of desired.
maxUnavailable cannot be 0 when maxSurge is 0, and maxSurge cannot be 0 when maxUnavailable is 0, so at least one of the two must allow change.
minReadySeconds is how long a new Pod must be ready without any container crashing before it counts as available; it defaults to 0, so a ready Pod is available at once.

Rolling update Deployments can run several versions at once; if scaled mid-rollout, the controller spreads the extra replicas across the active ReplicaSets, giving bigger shares to those with more replicas, to mitigate risk.

definition.text: A Kubernetes Service type says how a Service is exposed: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer or ExternalName, with headless Services as a variant.

facts.text: ClusterIP, the default, exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP so it is reachable only from within the cluster; an Ingress or Gateway can expose it to the public internet.
NodePort exposes the Service on each Node's IP at a static port: the control plane allocates one from a range (default 30000-32767) and every node proxies that same port into the Service.
LoadBalancer exposes the Service externally through a load balancer; Kubernetes offers no load balancing component itself, so you provide one or integrate with a cloud provider.

A LoadBalancer Service typically starts as a NodePort Service, and the cloud-controller-manager then configures the external load balancer to forward traffic to that node port; creation is asynchronous.
ExternalName maps the Service to a DNS name by returning a CNAME record for the external hostname; no proxying of any kind is set up.
The type field is nested functionality, each level adding to the previous: several types build on ClusterIP as a foundation.
A headless Service sets the cluster IP to None: no cluster IP is allocated, kube-proxy ignores it, and DNS returns individual Pod IPs so a client can connect to whichever Pod it prefers.
Ingress is not a Service type but an entry point for HTTP traffic that consolidates routing rules into one resource, exposing several components behind a single listener.

definition.text: An Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services inside it, using rules defined on the Ingress resource.

facts.text: Ingress exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services inside it, and the rules defined on the Ingress resource control how traffic is routed.
An Ingress can give Services externally reachable URLs, load balance traffic, terminate SSL/TLS and offer name-based virtual hosting.
An Ingress controller fulfils the Ingress, usually with a load balancer; without a controller, creating an Ingress resource has no effect.
Each rule has an optional host and a list of paths, each with a backend naming a Service and port; both host and path must match before traffic is sent to that Service.
A fanout setup routes traffic from a single IP address to more than one Service based on the requested URI, which keeps the number of load balancers to a minimum.
An Ingress is secured with a Secret holding a TLS private key and certificate; it supports only TLS port 443 and terminates TLS at the ingress point, so traffic to Services and Pods is plaintext.

Advanced load balancing such as persistent sessions and dynamic weights is not exposed through Ingress; it comes from the load balancer used for a Service, and readiness probes stand in for health checks.
An Ingress does not expose arbitrary ports or protocols; services other than HTTP and HTTPS are usually exposed with a Service of type NodePort or LoadBalancer.

definition.text: Ingress rules choose a backend by matching the request's host and URL path, using a path type of Exact, Prefix or ImplementationSpecific.

facts.text: Every path needs a pathType, and a path without one fails validation; Exact matches the URL path exactly and case-sensitively, while Prefix matches element by element on the path split by slashes.
Prefix /foo/bar matches /foo/bar/baz but not /foo/barbaz; when several paths match, the longest matching path wins, and between equal matches an Exact path beats a Prefix path.
A host can be exact, such as foo.bar.com, or a wildcard such as *.foo.com, which covers a single DNS label; name-based virtual hosting routes several host names at one IP address by the Host header.
Requests that match no host or path go to the default backend, and an Ingress with no rules must specify one; if none is set, the controller decides how to handle them.

definition.text: An Ingress controller carries out the Ingress rules, and an IngressClass tells each Ingress which controller should implement it.

facts.text: An Ingress controller must be running to satisfy an Ingress; many are available, and although all should fit the reference specification, in reality they operate slightly differently.
Ingresses can be implemented by different controllers, so each should name an IngressClass, a resource that carries extra configuration including the name of the controller that implements the class.

An IngressClass can reference a parameters resource that is cluster-scoped by default or namespaced; namespaced parameters let the cluster operator delegate control of settings such as load balancer configuration to a workload's team.
One IngressClass can be marked as the cluster default and is assigned to Ingresses without a class; with more than one default, the admission controller rejects new Ingresses that lack a class name.

definition.text: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler automatically updates a workload resource such as a Deployment or StatefulSet to scale capacity to match demand.

facts.text: Horizontal scaling responds to increased load by deploying more Pods, unlike vertical scaling, which would give the running Pods more memory or CPU.
When load falls and the Pod count is above the configured minimum, the autoscaler scales the workload back down; it does not apply to objects that cannot be scaled, such as a DaemonSet.
It is an API resource plus a controller in the control plane, running a control loop intermittently rather than continuously, by default every 15 seconds.

Each period the controller reads metrics through the resource metrics API, usually provided by Metrics Server, or the custom metrics API; a utilization target is a percentage of the Pod's resource request.
The core calculation is desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue): a current value of 200m against a desired 100m doubles the replicas, and 50m halves them.
The control plane skips scaling when the ratio is close enough to 1.0, within a configurable tolerance that defaults to 0.1.
With several metrics, each is evaluated and the largest desired replica count is used, up to the configured maximum.
An autoscaler is bound to one Deployment and manages its replicas field; spec.replicas should be removed from the manifest, or each kubectl apply resets the count and causes flapping.

definition.text: Autoscaler flapping controls are settings that keep the replica count from swinging up and down as metrics fluctuate.

facts.text: Replica counts can fluctuate frequently as the evaluated metrics change, which is called thrashing or flapping and is similar to hysteresis.

On scale-down the autoscaler uses the highest desired count from a stabilization window, a rolling maximum, so it does not remove Pods only to recreate them moments later; the default window is 300 seconds.

Scaling policies cap the rate of change as a number of Pods or a percentage per period; the policy allowing the largest change is chosen by default, Min picks the smallest, and Disabled turns scaling off in that direction.

By default scale-up has no stabilization window and adds at most 4 Pods or 100% of the running replicas every 15 seconds; a tolerance makes the autoscaler ignore metric changes inside a threshold, 10% by default.

definition.text: Scaling to zero lets an autoscaler reduce an idle workload to no replicas and bring it back when a metric shows demand.

facts.text: An autoscaler that scales on custom (object) or external metrics can set minReplicas to 0, so the workload drops to zero replicas with no load and scales back up when the metric shows a replica is needed.
It suits workloads that sit idle for long periods and are expensive to keep running, such as consumers of an occasionally used queue or jobs needing dedicated hardware like GPUs.
It is not available for resource metrics such as CPU or memory, which can only be measured on running Pods, and the API server rejects minReplicas 0 without at least one object or external metric.
While a workload is held at zero the autoscaler sets a ScaledToZero condition, which tells it apart from a workload someone deactivated manually by setting its replicas to 0.

definition.text: A pod template is the specification a workload controller uses to create the Pods it manages.

facts.text: Controllers for workload resources such as Deployments, Jobs and DaemonSets create Pods from a pod template included in the workload object, and the template is part of the workload's desired state.
Changing a pod template has no direct effect on existing Pods: the controller creates replacement Pods from the new template instead of patching the old ones, until all old Pods are replaced.

Each workload resource has its own rules for template changes, and the kubelet never sees templates; this separation of concerns simplifies the semantics and lets the cluster's behavior be extended without changing existing code.

A running Pod can be edited in place only a little: most metadata is immutable, and only container images, the active deadline, termination grace period, scheduling gates and added tolerations can change.

definition.text: A Pod can hold several tightly coupled containers, such as init containers that run first and sidecar containers that support the main application.

facts.text: Pods support multiple cooperating containers that are co-located, co-scheduled and share resources, but the most common case is one container per Pod, with Kubernetes managing the Pod rather than the container.
In a typical multi-container Pod, one container serves files from a shared volume to the public while a separate sidecar container refreshes those files from a remote source.

Sidecar containers provide auxiliary services to the main application, such as a service mesh; an init container with restartPolicy Always is a sidecar that starts before the application and runs until the Pod shuts down.
Init containers, by default, run to completion before the application containers start.

definition.text: A container can declare how much CPU and memory it needs and how much it may use, which drives scheduling and enforcement.

facts.text: When specifying a Pod, you can optionally state how much of each resource a container needs; the most common resources are CPU and memory (RAM).
The kube-scheduler uses the resource requests of a Pod's containers to decide which node to place the Pod on.
The kubelet enforces limits so a running container cannot use more than its limit: CPU limits by throttling, where the kernel restricts CPU access, and memory limits by out-of-memory kills.

Autoscaling measures utilization as current usage divided by the Pod's requested resources, so requests must be set; if a container lacks a request, CPU utilization is undefined and the autoscaler takes no action.
Kubernetes can change a Pod's CPU and memory after creation in two ways: resizing the running Pod in place, or changing the pod template so the workload's controller launches replacement Pods.

In-place resize updates the desired state through the /resize subresource and the kubelet applies it to running containers; only CPU and memory can be resized, the QoS class stays fixed, and resizePolicy says whether a restart is needed.

Resizing by replacement works on any Kubernetes version and can change any Pod specification, but it replaces Pods, so the workload must tolerate planned disruptions and a PodDisruptionBudget can control availability.

definition.text: A probe is a periodic check the kubelet runs on a container, so Kubernetes can restart the container when it is unhealthy or stop sending it traffic when it is not ready.

facts.text: A probe is a diagnostic the kubelet performs periodically on a container, by running code inside it or making a network request; the results let Kubernetes restart unhealthy containers or stop sending traffic to containers that are not ready.

An exec probe runs a command in the container through the container runtime and treats exit code 0 as healthy; a TCP probe, checked directly by the kubelet, is healthy only if a connection to the port opens.

An HTTP probe sends a GET request and counts any status from 200 up to but not including 400 as success, anything else as failure; a gRPC probe uses the gRPC Health Checking Protocol, and every error is a failure.

Liveness probes decide when to restart a container, for example one that is deadlocked and cannot progress; after more failures than the configured tolerance the kubelet restarts it. initialDelaySeconds delays the first probe and periodSeconds sets the interval.

Readiness probes decide when a container can accept traffic, covering slow startup work such as warming caches and later overloads; a failing probe gets the Pod's IP removed from the EndpointSlices of every matching Service.

A startup probe checks whether the application has started and runs only at startup; until it succeeds no liveness or readiness probes run, and if it fails the kubelet kills the container and applies its restart policy.

For a slow-starting application, give the startup probe the same check with failureThreshold times periodSeconds long enough for the worst-case startup, such as 30 * 10 = 300s; liveness then takes over for fast reaction to deadlocks.

Ingress exposes no health checks, but readiness probes achieve the same end result. Autoscaling ignores a starting Pod's CPU for an initialization period, 5 minutes by default, so a startup or readiness probe should pass only after any spike.

definition.text: Release engineering is the discipline of building and delivering software, defining every step from source storage and build rules to testing, packaging and deployment.

facts.text: Running reliable services requires reliable release processes: binaries and configurations are built reproducibly and automatically, so releases are repeatable rather than unique snowflakes, and changes to the release process are intentional.
In the self-service model, product teams control and run their own release processes and decide how often to release; releases are automated until problems need an engineer.

High velocity rests on the view that frequent releases mean fewer changes between versions, which makes testing and troubleshooting easier; some teams build hourly and pick the build to deploy from test results.
Several layers of access control gate who can approve source changes, create a release, approve cherry picks, deploy a release or change build configuration, and almost all changes need code review.
An archived report of all changes in a release helps SREs troubleshoot a problem release faster.
Release engineers and SREs together develop strategies for canarying changes, pushing new releases without interrupting services, and rolling back features that show problems.

Teams should budget for release engineering at the start of product development, because putting good practice in place early is cheaper than retrofitting it, and developers, SREs and release engineers should work together.

definition.text: A release pipeline turns a tested source revision into a deployable package by branching, building, testing, packaging and canarying, logging each step.

facts.text: A continuous test system runs unit tests on the mainline at every submitted change, and releases are cut at the revision of the last continuous test build that passed all tests, so release-time builds are less likely to fail.
The pipeline creates a release branch from the requested integration revision, then compiles the binaries and runs unit tests, often in parallel, in environments dedicated to those tasks.
Unit tests are re-run on the release branch with an audit trail, because cherry picks can leave a branch with code that exists nowhere on the mainline.
Packages are named, versioned with a unique hash and signed; labels such as dev, canary and production mark a package's place in the release, and reapplying a label moves it to the newest package.
Build artifacts then go to system testing and canary deployments; a typical canary starts a few jobs in production after system tests finish.
Each step's result is logged and a report of all changes since the last release is created.

definition.text: Release branching cuts a branch from the mainline at one revision and fixes it only by cherry-picking bug fixes, so the release contents stay known.

facts.text: All code is checked into the mainline, but most major projects release from a branch cut at a specific revision, and changes are never merged from the branch back into the mainline.
Bug fixes go to the mainline first and are then cherry picked into the release branch, which avoids picking up unrelated mainline changes and means the exact contents of each release are known.
To fix a bug in an older release, rebuild at the same revision as the original build and include the specific later changes; this tactic is called cherry picking.
Cherry pick requests are approved or rejected individually for inclusion in a release, and a release system manages the release branches and cherry picks.

definition.text: A hermetic build is insensitive to the software installed on the build machine, so the same revision always produces the same result.

facts.text: Building the same product at the same source revision on different machines should give identical results, so builds are insensitive to the libraries and other software installed on the build machine.
Hermetic builds depend on known versions of build tools such as compilers and of dependencies such as libraries, and are self-contained, relying on no services external to the build environment.

Build tools are themselves versioned by source revision, so a project built last month does not use this month's compiler when a cherry pick forces a rebuild, since that compiler may have incompatible features.
Every binary can display its build date, revision number and build identifier, tying it to a record of how it was built.

definition.text: Configuration can reach a running service in several ways, each trading flexibility, simplicity and drift between the stored and running version.

facts.text: Configuration changes are a potential source of instability, so every distribution scheme stores configuration in the main source repository and enforces strict code review.

Mainline: changes to configuration files at the head of the main branch are reviewed and then applied to the running system, decoupling binary releases from configuration, but the running version can skew from the checked-in one.
Same package: shipping configuration files in the binary's package binds the two tightly and limits flexibility, but simplifies deployment because only one package is installed.

Separate configuration packages: snapshotting configuration alongside its binary lets each change independently, so a wrong feature flag value can be fixed by cherry picking, rebuilding the configuration package and deploying, without a new binary.
External store: configuration that must change often or while the binary is running can be read from an external store such as Chubby, Bigtable or a source-based filesystem.
Project owners weigh these options and choose case by case.

definition.text: A risk-based rollout fits how fast and how widely a release is pushed to the risk profile of the service being updated.

facts.text: The goal is to fit the deployment process to a service's risk profile; in development or pre-production, builds can run hourly and be pushed automatically when all tests pass.
For large user-facing services, a push starts in one cluster and expands exponentially until all clusters are updated.
For sensitive infrastructure, the rollout may stretch over several days, interleaving instances in different geographic regions.
A rollout is a logical unit of work made of tasks; automation can update all jobs at once or roll a new binary out to successive clusters over hours, with a dashboard to control and monitor it.

definition.text: A Pod starts in the Pending phase, moves to Running once at least one primary container starts, and ends in Succeeded or Failed depending on whether any container terminated in failure.

facts.text: Pods are relatively ephemeral: each is created with a unique UID, scheduled (bound) to a node only once, and stays there until termination according to restart policy or deletion.

The phase is a high-level summary, not a state machine: Pending means accepted but containers not yet set up, including waiting to be scheduled and downloading images; Running means bound to a node with a container running or starting.

Succeeded means all containers terminated in success and will not be restarted; Failed means all terminated and at least one failed, by non-zero exit or system kill; Unknown means the state could not be obtained, typically a node communication error.
Each container is Waiting (still pulling the image or applying Secret data), Running (executing, any postStart hook finished) or Terminated (ran to completion or failed; a preStop hook runs first).

The kubelet records Pod conditions: PodScheduled, PodReadyToStartContainers, Initialized (all init containers completed), ContainersReady, and Ready, meaning the Pod can serve requests and joins the load balancing pools of all matching Services.
Readiness gates add custom conditions to Pod readiness: a Pod is Ready only when all its containers are ready and every gate condition is True, and a condition that cannot be found defaults to False.

The kubelet may restart a failed container, but a Pod that fails unrecoverably, sits on a failed node or is evicted is deleted; a controller manages these disposable Pods; a dead node's Pods are marked for removal after a timeout.

A Pod is never rescheduled: a near-identical replacement with a new UID, possibly the same name, takes over, maybe on another node, and anything tied to the old Pod's lifetime, such as a volume, is recreated.

title: Pod restart policy
article: doc>kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle#How Pods handle problems with containers > Container restarts > Pod-level container restart policy

definition.text: The restartPolicy in a Pod spec tells Kubernetes whether to restart a container after it exits, and can be Always, OnFailure or Never.

facts.text: A Pod's restartPolicy is Always, OnFailure or Never, with Always the default; it governs how Kubernetes reacts to containers exiting and applies to app containers and regular init containers.
Always restarts a container after any termination; OnFailure restarts it only if it exits with an error (non-zero exit status); Never does not automatically restart a terminated container.

Sidecar containers ignore the Pod-level policy because a sidecar is an init container whose own restartPolicy is Always; a restart is not always appropriate, since regular init containers run only once during startup.

Individual containers can override the Pod policy with their own restartPolicy and ordered restartPolicyRules that compare the exit code with listed values; the first match applies Restart, and with no match the container's policy applies.

Restart rules can separate restartable from non-restartable errors, for example a Never Pod whose container restarts only on specific exit codes, or an Always Pod whose one-shot init container fails the Pod if setup fails.

The RestartAllContainers action restarts the whole Pod in place: all containers stop without honoring the grace period or preStop hooks, init containers re-run, and the Pod keeps its UID, IP address, sandbox and volumes.

In-place restart suits workloads where rescheduling is costly, such as batch jobs or AI/ML training, and lets a sidecar watcher reset the application to a known-good state by exiting with a chosen code.

The Kubernetes project recommends resilient design that accounts for unannounced restarts, either by failing the Pod and relying on automatic replacement or by container-level resilience, so the workload stays available despite partial failure.

definition.text: CrashLoopBackOff is the condition of a container that fails to start properly and keeps failing and restarting while Kubernetes delays each restart with an exponential backoff.

facts.text: After a container's first crash Kubernetes restarts it immediately; repeated crashes get an exponential backoff delay, which stops a faulty container from overwhelming the system with failed start attempts.

Restart delays start at 10s and double each time up to a default cap of 300s (5 minutes), which the kubelet's maxContainerRestartPeriod can lower to 1s; running successfully for a duration such as 10 minutes resets the delay.

Typical causes are application errors, configuration errors such as wrong environment variables or missing files, too little memory or CPU, and health checks failing because the application does not start serving in time, including liveness or startup probe failures.
To investigate, read the container logs with kubectl logs, inspect Pod events with kubectl describe pod, review configuration and resource limits, and run the image locally to debug the application.

title: Graceful pod termination

definition.text: When a Pod is deleted, the kubelet first asks its containers to stop with a TERM signal and only sends KILL once a grace period has expired, so processes can clean up.

facts.text: Pods are processes, so they should terminate gracefully rather than be abruptly stopped with a KILL signal; the design aim is that you can request deletion and know when processes end, while deletes still eventually complete.
When you request deletion, the cluster records the intended grace period before the Pod may be forcefully killed, and the kubelet then attempts graceful shutdown.

The kubelet has the container runtime send a TERM (SIGTERM) signal, with a grace period timeout, to each container's main process; after the grace period KILL goes to remaining processes and the Pod is deleted from the API server.
A container's preStop hook runs before the container enters the Terminated state, while an in-place Pod restart skips the grace period and preStop hooks for a swift shutdown.

notes: thin: the lifecycle page only summarizes termination; the default grace period, custom stop signals, forced deletion, sidecar shutdown order and garbage collection of terminated Pods are on a separate Termination of Pods page that is not crawled.
